paragraph.en:
Helmet with Visor

The shape of this multipeaked visor was designed to deflect blows or sword cuts.

The helmet was originally fitted inside with a padded lining that added both comfort and protection for the wearer’s head.

paragraph.en:
Sword

After the initial charge resulted in a lost or broken lance, the man-at-arms might draw his sword to defend himself in closely packed battle conditions. Copper inlay of the mark of the bishop’s crosier or staff indicates that it was made in Passau, a renowned South German sword-making center.

paragraph.en:
Breastplate

Fashion trends dictated the shape and decoration of the breastplate. The low neckline and billowing chest with gathered and pleated fabric seen in this portrait from about 1515 are translated into hard steel.

content.caption: Follower of Giovanni di Niccolò de Luteri (Dosso Dossi) Bust-Length Portrait of a Man, 16th century.

paragraph.en:
Mail Sleeves

These sleeves were tailored and sewn to the padded undergarment or doublet. When a soldier raised his arm his armpit was exposed. Mail was the ideal flexible armor for this vulnerable area. These brass rings in the center of the armpit are believed to be talismanic, meant to ward off attacks from soldiers below.
